q: What is the main objective of criminal investigation?
a: To identify, locate and prove the guilt of the offender
To punish the offender as quickly as possible
To obtain a confession from every suspect
To collect fines from persons who break the law
r: Criminal investigation aims to identify the offender, trace and locate him, and gather evidence to prove his guilt in court.
Punishment is imposed by the court after trial, not by investigators.
A confession is not required and must never be the only aim.
Fines are imposed by courts, not collected through investigation.
e: The three phases of investigation follow these objectives.

q: Which tool of investigation refers to the use of scientific instruments and forensic methods?
a: Instrumentation
Information
Interrogation
Identification
r: Instrumentation is the application of instruments and methods of the physical sciences to detect crime.
Information is the knowledge gathered from persons and records.
Interrogation is the skillful questioning of suspects and witnesses.
Identification is an objective of investigation, not one of the three tools.
e: The three I's of investigation are information, interrogation (with interview) and instrumentation.

q: Which cardinal point of investigation deals with the motive for the crime?
a: Why
How
When
Where
r: 'Why' asks for the reason or motive behind the crime.
'How' asks for the manner in which the crime was committed.
'When' asks for the time of the crime.
'Where' asks for the place of the crime.
e: The six cardinal points are what, where, when, how, who and why.

q: Why must intelligence be timely?
a: It loses its value if it reaches users after they must act
Late intelligence is always more accurate than early intelligence
Timeliness matters only for military, not police, intelligence
Intelligence is useful only after the operation is over
r: Intelligence exists to support decisions and operations; if it arrives late, it cannot influence them.
Delay does not make intelligence more accurate.
Timeliness applies to all intelligence, including police intelligence.
Intelligence is meant to guide operations before and during them.
e: Other principles of intelligence include usefulness, security and continuity.

q: A suspect confessed during investigation. Why is the third phase of investigation, proving guilt, still not complete?
a: A confession needs evidence of the corpus delicti to support a conviction
A confession can never be used as evidence against anyone
The third phase needs a second confession from the suspect
The third phase begins only after the suspect is convicted
r: Under Rule 133, an extrajudicial confession is not enough to convict without evidence of the corpus delicti.
A valid confession is admissible; it simply needs corroboration.
No rule requires a second confession.
Proof of guilt is gathered before trial, not after conviction.
e: Investigators should gather physical and testimonial evidence that stands on its own.

q: An agent watches a suspected drug den from a rented room across the street for several days. What type of surveillance is this?
a: Stakeout (fixed surveillance)
Tailing (moving surveillance)
Roping (undercover work)
Casing of a target
r: A stakeout is fixed surveillance of a place from a stationary position.
Tailing follows a moving subject on foot or by vehicle.
Roping is undercover work where the agent assumes a role to gain the subject's confidence.
Casing is the inspection of a place to plan an operation.
e: Surveillance is the covert observation of persons, places or things to obtain information.

q: Finished intelligence is delivered to the commander who requested it so he can plan an operation. Which phase of the intelligence cycle is this?
a: Dissemination and use
Planning and direction
Collection
Processing
r: Dissemination delivers the finished intelligence to the users who need it.
Planning and direction decides what intelligence is needed.
Collection gathers the raw information.
Processing records, evaluates and interprets the information.
e: The cycle starts again as new needs arise.

q: A source has always been reliable, and his report is confirmed by other sources. How should the information be rated?
r: A means completely reliable source; 1 means confirmed by other sources.
B-2 means usually reliable and probably true.
C-3 means fairly reliable and possibly true.
F-6 means the source's reliability and the truth cannot be judged.
e: Letters rate the source (A to F); numbers rate the information (1 to 6).

q: A man regularly gives the police information about a gang in exchange for money. How is he classified?
a: As an informer, because he gives information for a fee
As an informant, because he gives information once and freely
As a witness, because he will surely testify in court
As an undercover agent, because he is a police officer
r: An informer furnishes information regularly, usually for a fee or reward.
An informant gives information freely, often once, without seeking reward.
Informers usually do not testify, to protect their identity.
He is a private person, not a police officer.
e: Investigators must protect the identity of informers and weigh their motives.

q: Unauthorized disclosure of a document would cause grave, but not exceptionally grave, damage to the nation. How should it be classified?
a: Secret
Top Secret
Confidential
Restricted
r: Secret covers information whose disclosure would cause grave damage.
Top Secret covers exceptionally grave damage.
Confidential covers damage or prejudice to the interest of the nation.
Restricted covers information for official use only.
e: Classification decides who may have access and how the document is handled.

q: A body was found in a large open field. Several officers will search the area. Which search method is most suitable?
a: Strip (line) method
Spiral (circle) method
Wheel method
Zone method
r: In the strip or line method, searchers walk side by side in straight lines, which covers large open areas well.
The spiral method is used by one searcher moving in or out in circles.
The wheel method has searchers move out from the center like spokes; it can leave gaps.
The zone method divides a place, such as a house, into sections.
e: The choice of method depends on the size and nature of the scene and the number of searchers.

q: A house with several rooms is divided into sections, and each section is assigned to a searcher. Which search method is this?
a: Zone (quadrant) method
Strip (line) method
Spiral method
Wheel method
r: The zone or quadrant method divides the scene into sections that are searched one at a time or by different searchers.
The strip method is for open areas searched in lines.
The spiral method is for one searcher moving in circles.
The wheel method moves out from a central point.
e: Each zone should be searched thoroughly and recorded before moving on.

q: An investigator wants one drawing to show the bloodstains on the floor and on the four walls of a room. Which sketch should he make?
a: Cross-projection (exploded) sketch
Locality (vicinity) sketch
Perspective (3-D) sketch
Rough sketch only
r: A cross-projection sketch folds the walls down flat around the floor so marks on them can be shown together.
A locality sketch shows the scene and its surroundings, such as nearby roads.
A perspective sketch shows the scene in three dimensions.
A rough sketch is the first sketch made at the scene; it does not by itself solve the problem.
e: The finished sketch is drawn to scale from the rough sketch and measurements.

q: Why can a confession obtained through torture not be used as evidence, even if it is true?
a: R.A. 9745 makes it inadmissible, except against the torturer
It is admissible if the suspect later repeats it in court
It is admissible if the torture left no visible injuries
It is admissible if the crime is a heinous one
r: Section 8 of R.A. 9745 excludes any statement obtained through torture, except when used against the person accused of torture.
Repeating it in court does not cure the original illegality of the extrajudicial confession.
Mental torture leaves no visible marks and is still torture.
No crime, however grave, allows the use of torture.
e: The exclusion removes any incentive to torture suspects.

q: A store owner catches a man in the act of stealing and holds him. Was the arrest lawful, and what must the owner do next?
a: Lawful; he must hand the man to the nearest police station without delay
Unlawful, because only police officers may arrest anyone
Lawful; he may keep the man in the store until the next day
Unlawful, unless the owner first obtains a warrant
r: A private person may arrest an offender caught in the act and must deliver him to the nearest police station or jail without unnecessary delay.
Private persons may arrest in the cases under Rule 113, Sec. 5.
Keeping the person longer than necessary may be illegal detention.
No warrant is needed for an in flagrante delicto arrest.
e: A citizen's arrest is subject to the same rules on warrantless arrest.
l: Rules of Court, Rule 113, Secs. 5 and 9

q: A woman reports that she was raped an hour ago. What should the investigator advise her before the medico-legal examination?
a: Do not bathe or change clothes, so physical evidence is preserved
Bathe first so she will feel comfortable during the examination
Wash the clothes she wore before bringing them to the police
Wait a week before the examination so she can rest
r: Bathing or changing clothes can destroy semen, hair, fibers and other evidence.
Comfort matters, but evidence must be preserved first.
Washing the clothes destroys evidence.
Delay lets injuries heal and evidence disappear.
e: Rape victims are referred to the Women and Children Protection Desk and handled with sensitivity.
l: R.A. 8505 (Rape Victim Assistance and Protection Act)

q: The first officer at a stabbing scene finds the victim still breathing. What should he do first?
a: Give or call for medical aid, then secure the scene
Search the victim's pockets for evidence
Take photographs before anything else
Look for the suspect in the nearby streets
r: Saving life comes first; the officer then protects the scene and the evidence.
Searching the victim delays aid and may disturb evidence.
Photographs are important, but not before life-saving aid.
Leaving the victim to chase a suspect abandons the first duty.
e: If the victim is moved for treatment, the officer notes his original position.

q: A fraternity member was present during a hazing in which a neophyte died, but did nothing to stop it. How does R.A. 11053 treat his presence?
a: As prima facie evidence that he took part as a principal
As proof that he was only a witness and is not liable
As a mitigating circumstance in favor of the member
As irrelevant unless he struck the neophyte himself
r: R.A. 11053 makes presence during hazing prima facie evidence of participation as a principal, unless he tried to prevent it or promptly reported it.
Presence is not treated as merely being a witness.
Presence is not a mitigating circumstance under the law.
The law punishes participation, and presence raises a presumption of it.
e: Officers and members who planned or took part in hazing face heavy penalties, especially if death results.

q: Co-workers of equal rank keep making sexual remarks about a colleague at the office. Which law most directly applies?
a: R.A. 11313, which covers peer harassment at work
R.A. 7877, which requires authority over the victim
R.A. 9262, which covers intimate partners only
R.A. 11053, which covers initiation rites
r: The Safe Spaces Act covers gender-based sexual harassment in workplaces, including between peers.
R.A. 7877 applies when the offender has authority, influence or moral ascendancy over the victim.
R.A. 9262 concerns violence against women in intimate relationships.
R.A. 11053 concerns hazing.
e: R.A. 11313 extended protection to streets, public spaces, online spaces, workplaces and schools.

q: A wife is suspected of killing her husband. Beyond the evidence needed for homicide, what must investigators also obtain?
a: Proof of their marriage, such as the marriage certificate
Proof that the husband had no life insurance
Proof that the wife had a previous criminal record
Proof that the killing happened at their home
r: Parricide requires the relationship; the marriage certificate is the best evidence of it.
Insurance is not an element of parricide.
A prior record is not an element of the crime.
The place of the killing is not an element of parricide.
e: The relationship must also be alleged in the information.

q: How does somatic death differ from molecular death?
a: Somatic is the stop of vital functions; molecular is the later death of cells
Somatic is the death of cells; molecular is the stop of breathing
Somatic happens days after molecular death
Somatic applies to animals; molecular applies to humans
r: Somatic (clinical) death is the complete and continuous stop of brain, heart and lung functions; molecular (cellular) death follows hours later.
This reverses the two kinds of death.
Somatic death comes first, then molecular death.
Both apply to humans.
e: The gap between somatic and molecular death explains why organs can be harvested for transplant.

q: A body found lying face down has fixed lividity on its back. What does this suggest?
a: The body was moved after the lividity had become fixed
The victim died lying face down where he was found
The victim died less than an hour ago
The lividity was caused by blows before death
r: Lividity settles in the lowest parts; if it is fixed on the back while the body faces down, the body was turned or moved.
Death face down would put the lividity on the front.
Fixed lividity takes several hours to develop.
Lividity is a post-mortem change, not a bruise from blows.
e: Livor mortis helps estimate the time of death and detect movement of the body.

q: A wound has clean, sharp edges and is longer than it is deep. What kind of wound is it?
a: Incised wound
Stab wound
Lacerated wound
Punctured wound
r: An incised wound is made by a sharp edge drawn across the skin; it is longer than deep.
A stab wound is deeper than it is long.
A lacerated wound has irregular, torn edges from blunt force.
A punctured wound is made by a pointed instrument without a cutting edge.
e: The type of wound suggests the kind of weapon used.

q: A body has two gunshot wounds. Which features point to the wound of entrance?
a: Smaller size, inverted edges and a contusion collar
Larger size, everted edges and no contusion collar
Ragged edges with tissue pushed outward
No difference between entrance and exit
r: Entrance wounds are usually smaller, with edges pushed inward and a ring of abrasion or contusion.
These describe an exit wound.
Outward-pushed tissue describes an exit wound.
Entrance and exit wounds usually show clear differences.
e: Close-range wounds may also show burning, smudging or tattooing from powder.

q: Under magnification, strands of tissue bridge the depth of a wound with irregular edges. What does this indicate?
a: A laceration from blunt force, not a sharp cut
An incised wound from a very sharp knife
A gunshot wound from a long distance
A burn from a hot object
r: Tissue bridges remain when blunt force tears the skin; sharp instruments cut through everything cleanly.
Sharp weapons leave no tissue bridges.
Gunshot wounds have distinct features such as a contusion collar.
Burns do not form tissue bridges.
e: Telling lacerations from cuts helps identify the weapon.

q: How does an interview differ from an interrogation?
a: An interview questions willing persons; an interrogation questions reluctant suspects
An interview is only for suspects; an interrogation only for victims
An interview is always recorded; an interrogation never is
An interview is done in court; an interrogation at the scene
r: Interviews gather information from those willing to share it, such as witnesses; interrogations question suspects or reluctant persons.
Both may involve various persons, but interviews usually involve witnesses and victims.
Both may be recorded.
Neither is done in court; both are investigative.
e: Rights of persons under custodial investigation apply during interrogation of suspects.

q: One investigator acts harsh toward the suspect while another acts kind and offers to help him. Which technique is this?
a: Mutt and Jeff
Bluff on a split pair
Stern approach
Extenuation
r: Mutt and Jeff uses one hostile and one friendly investigator so the suspect turns to the friendly one.
Bluff on a split pair tells one suspect that his partner has already confessed.
The stern approach uses a firm, businesslike manner by one investigator.
Extenuation reduces the moral seriousness of the act to encourage a confession.
e: All techniques must respect the suspect's rights; threats and torture are unlawful.

q: A suspect says he was at the scene and owns the knife found there, but denies killing the victim. What is his statement?
a: An admission
A confession
A dying declaration
A res gestae statement
r: An admission acknowledges facts that tend to prove guilt, without admitting the crime itself.
A confession acknowledges guilt of the offense.
A dying declaration is made by a victim conscious of impending death.
A res gestae statement is made spontaneously during or right after a startling event.
e: Admissions and confessions under custodial investigation must follow the rules of R.A. 7438.
l: Rules of Court, Rule 130, Secs. 27 and 34

q: A witness testifies that she heard the accused shout threats at the victim, offered only to prove that the words were spoken. How is this testimony treated?
a: As an independent relevant statement, not hearsay
As hearsay that must be excluded
As a dying declaration of the victim
As an extrajudicial confession of the accused
r: When the fact that words were said is itself relevant, not their truth, the statement is an independent relevant statement.
Hearsay applies only when the statement is offered to prove its truth.
A dying declaration is made by the victim about his own death.
Threats are not a confession of a crime.
e: The witness heard the words personally, so she can testify that they were said.

q: Without counsel, a suspect confessed orally to an officer during custodial investigation. The officer later testifies about it. Is the confession admissible?
a: No, because it was made without counsel and not in writing
Yes, because the officer heard it personally
Yes, because oral confessions need no counsel
No, unless the suspect repeats it in a newspaper interview
r: R.A. 7438 requires an extrajudicial confession in custody to be in writing and signed with counsel, or with a valid waiver before the persons the law names.
Personal knowledge of the officer does not cure the violation of the suspect's rights.
Custodial confessions, oral or written, require the assistance of counsel.
A media interview does not make the custodial confession admissible.
e: Spontaneous statements to the media, not made during custodial investigation, are treated differently.
l: R.A. 7438, Sec. 2(d); 1987 Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 12

q: In money laundering, which stage moves dirty money through many transactions to hide its source?
a: Layering
Placement
Integration
Structuring
r: Layering separates the money from its source through complex transfers and transactions.
Placement is putting the cash into the financial system.
Integration returns the money to the economy as apparently legitimate funds.
Structuring is splitting deposits to avoid reporting thresholds, a placement method.
e: R.A. 9160, as amended, created the Anti-Money Laundering Council.

q: A man drove away a parked car without the owner's consent, intending to sell it. What crime did he commit?
a: Carnapping under R.A. 10883
Simple theft under the Revised Penal Code
Robbery with force upon things
Estafa through abuse of confidence
r: R.A. 10883 defines carnapping as taking a motor vehicle of another, with intent to gain, without consent or by violence, intimidation or force.
The special law on carnapping applies to motor vehicles.
Carnapping covers the taking of motor vehicles whatever the means.
There was no abuse of confidence.
e: R.A. 10883 repealed R.A. 6539 and increased the penalties.

q: A shop owner bought a cellphone from a stranger at a very low price without a receipt and resold it. The phone was stolen. What is the owner's liability?
a: Fencing, with possession of the stolen item as prima facie evidence
Theft, because he had the stolen item in his store
None, because he paid for the cellphone
Estafa, because he resold the cellphone
r: P.D. 1612 punishes dealing in items one knows or should know were stolen; possession of stolen goods is prima facie evidence of fencing.
The fence is a different offender from the thief.
Paying for stolen goods is the very act of fencing.
Reselling stolen goods is fencing, not estafa.
e: A very low price and lack of receipt should alert a buyer that goods may be stolen.

q: A recruiter takes the passports of workers and forces them to work without pay. Which law applies?
a: The anti-trafficking law, R.A. 9208 as amended
The anti-carnapping law, R.A. 10883
The anti-fencing law, P.D. 1612
The anti-money laundering law, R.A. 9160
r: Recruiting and keeping persons for forced labor through coercion is trafficking in persons; confiscating passports is a punishable act.
R.A. 10883 concerns motor vehicles.
P.D. 1612 concerns stolen goods.
R.A. 9160 concerns laundering of proceeds of crime.
e: R.A. 9208 was expanded by R.A. 10364 and R.A. 11862.
l: R.A. 9208, as amended by R.A. 10364 and R.A. 11862

q: A company collector received payments from customers for his employer but kept the money. Why is he usually liable for qualified theft, not estafa?
a: He held the money only materially, not juridically
He used violence against the customers
He deceived the customers before they paid
He was not an employee of the company
r: An employee who receives money for the employer holds it only materially; taking it with grave abuse of confidence is qualified theft.
No violence was used.
Deceit of the customers is not shown.
He was an employee, which is why the abuse of confidence qualifies the theft.
e: Estafa by misappropriation requires juridical possession, as by an agent or trustee.

q: Which pillar of traffic management covers the design of roads and traffic control devices?
a: Traffic engineering
Traffic education
Traffic enforcement
Traffic economy
r: Engineering deals with road design, signs, signals and markings.
Education teaches road users safe behavior.
Enforcement applies traffic laws through apprehension.
Economy concerns the costs and benefits of the traffic system.
e: The five pillars are engineering, education, enforcement, environment and economy.

q: Why does the LTFRB, rather than the LTO, grant franchises to jeepneys and buses?
a: The LTFRB regulates public land transport services and their routes
The LTFRB registers all private cars and issues driver's licenses
The LTFRB designs and builds national highways
The LTFRB arrests drivers who violate traffic laws
r: The LTFRB issues franchises and regulates fares and routes of public utility vehicles.
Registration and licensing belong to the LTO.
Road design and construction belong to the DPWH.
Enforcement belongs to the PNP, MMDA and deputized officers.
e: Several agencies share traffic responsibilities, which calls for coordination.

q: An intersection has many accidents because drivers cannot see the cross traffic. Which response is most effective?
a: An engineering fix, such as clearing the view or adding signals
Posting more traffic enforcers there to issue tickets to drivers
A slogan contest on road safety in schools
Raising the fines for all traffic violations
r: The cause is a physical hazard, so changing the road environment addresses it directly.
Tickets do not remove the visibility problem.
Education helps but does not fix the hazard at that site.
Higher fines do not improve visibility.
e: Matching the pillar to the cause makes traffic management effective.

q: Which type of traffic sign warns drivers of a hazard ahead, such as a sharp curve?
a: Warning sign
Regulatory sign
Guide sign
Informative sign
r: Warning signs alert drivers to hazards or changes in road conditions ahead.
Regulatory signs state rules that must be obeyed, such as stop or no parking.
Guide signs show routes, directions and distances.
Informative signs give information about services and places.
e: Each category of sign has its own shape and color to be recognized quickly.

q: What does a broken white line between two lanes going the same way mean?
a: Lanes may be changed across it when safe
Drivers may never cross it for any reason
It marks the edge of the road
It marks a pedestrian crossing
r: Broken lines allow crossing when it is safe.
Solid lines discourage or prohibit crossing.
Edge lines are usually solid lines at the side of the road.
Pedestrian crossings are marked with wide stripes.
e: Road markings guide and regulate traffic together with signs and signals.

q: A driver is very close to the stop line when the light turns yellow, and stopping suddenly would be unsafe. What is the best action?
a: Proceed through with caution, since he cannot stop safely
Brake hard at once, whatever the cars behind him
Speed up to beat the red light at any cost
Stop in the middle of the intersection
r: Yellow warns that the light is about to turn red; a driver who cannot stop safely may proceed with caution.
Sudden hard braking may cause a rear-end collision.
Speeding up to beat the light is dangerous.
Stopping in the intersection blocks cross traffic.
e: Drivers approaching at a safe speed can usually stop when the light turns yellow.

q: Two cars reach an intersection without signals at about the same time. Under R.A. 4136, which car must yield?
a: The car on the left yields to the car on the right
The car on the right yields to the car on the left
The smaller car yields to the bigger one
The slower car yields to the faster one
r: R.A. 4136 provides that the vehicle on the left shall yield the right of way to the vehicle on the right.
This reverses the rule.
Size does not decide the right of way.
Speed does not decide the right of way.
e: Drivers on a through highway and emergency vehicles have special rules.

q: Where is a driver prohibited from parking under R.A. 4136?
a: On a pedestrian crosswalk
On a marked parking slot
In a private parking building
On a road shoulder where signs allow
r: R.A. 4136 prohibits parking on a crosswalk, within an intersection, and in other listed places.
Marked parking slots are meant for parking.
Private parking buildings are designed for parking.
Parking where signs allow is lawful.
e: Other prohibited places include within six meters of an intersection and in front of a private driveway.

q: A driver stopped at a red light reads and types a text message on his hand-held phone. Is this a violation of R.A. 10913?
a: Yes, the law also covers stops at a traffic light
No, because the vehicle was not moving
No, because texting is allowed at intersections
Yes, but only if the driver hits someone
r: R.A. 10913 covers using a hand-held device while in motion or temporarily stopped at a traffic light or intersection.
Being stopped at a light is expressly covered.
Intersections are expressly covered.
The violation is the act itself, without any accident.
e: Hands-free use is allowed if the device does not block the driver's view.

q: A father rides a motorcycle on a busy highway with his small child, whose feet cannot reach the foot pegs. Which law did he violate?
a: R.A. 10666, the Children's Safety on Motorcycles Act
R.A. 10586, the Anti-Drunk and Drugged Driving Act
R.A. 10913, the Anti-Distracted Driving Act
R.A. 4136, the rules on parking
r: R.A. 10666 bars a child from riding on public roads with heavy traffic unless the child can reach the foot pegs, wrap his arms around the driver, and wears a standard helmet.
R.A. 10586 concerns driving under the influence.
R.A. 10913 concerns distracted driving.
Parking rules do not apply to this situation.
e: There is an exception for medical emergencies.

q: An officer flags down a driver who was weaving between lanes and smells of liquor. What procedure should he follow?
a: Give field sobriety tests; if the driver fails, use a breath analyzer
Arrest him at once and take a blood sample by force
Let him go with a warning because no one was hurt
Ask the driver whether he is drunk and accept his answer
r: R.A. 10586 provides for field sobriety tests when there is probable cause, followed by a breath analyzer test if the driver fails.
The law sets the testing steps; force is not the procedure.
Driving under the influence is a violation even without an accident.
The driver's own answer is not a test.
e: Drivers in accidents causing death or serious injury undergo mandatory alcohol and drug tests.
l: R.A. 10586 (Anti-Drunk and Drugged Driving Act of 2013), Secs. 6-7

q: In traffic accident investigation, what is the point of no escape?
a: The point after which the accident can no longer be avoided
The point where the vehicle comes to rest after the crash
The point where the driver first sees the hazard
The point where the police first arrive at the scene
r: The point of no escape is the place and time after which nothing the driver does can prevent the accident.
The final position is where the vehicle stops after the crash.
The point of perception is when the driver first sees the hazard.
Police arrival is not part of the chain of key events.
e: Key events include perception, start of evasive action, point of no escape, maximum engagement and final position.

q: A collision injured two persons but killed no one. How is it classified?
a: Non-fatal injury accident
Fatal accident
Property damage only
Non-motor vehicle accident
r: An accident with injuries but no deaths is a non-fatal injury accident.
A fatal accident involves at least one death.
Property damage only means no injuries or deaths.
This was a motor vehicle collision.
e: Accident classification affects reporting and investigation priorities.

q: A pedestrian crossed carelessly, but the driver saw him in time and could have stopped, yet did not. Who is liable under the last clear chance doctrine?
a: The driver, who had the last chance to avoid the accident
The pedestrian, because he was careless first
Neither, because both were negligent
The owner of the road, for poor lighting
r: Under the last clear chance doctrine, the party who had the last fair opportunity to avoid the harm and failed is liable.
The pedestrian's earlier carelessness does not excuse the driver's later failure.
The doctrine decides liability when both were negligent.
Nothing shows the road's condition caused the accident.
e: The doctrine is applied in Philippine jurisprudence on vehicular accidents.

q: Curved, striated tire marks show that a car slid sideways while turning at high speed. What are these marks called?
a: Yaw marks
Skid marks
Scuff marks from a flat tire
Gouge marks
r: Yaw marks are curved marks left by tires sliding sideways while still rotating, as in a sharp turn at speed.
Skid marks are usually straight, made by locked wheels during braking.
Flat-tire marks are made by an underinflated tire, not by sliding sideways.
Gouges are made by metal parts digging into the road.
e: Yaw marks can be used to estimate the speed of the vehicle.

q: What does the fire tetrahedron add to the fire triangle?
a: An uninhibited chemical chain reaction
A source of ignition such as a spark
A supply of oxygen from the air
A fuel such as wood or gasoline
r: The tetrahedron adds the chain reaction that keeps the fire burning; breaking it extinguishes the fire.
Heat is already one side of the triangle.
Oxygen is already one side of the triangle.
Fuel is already one side of the triangle.
e: Some extinguishing agents, like dry chemicals, work by interrupting the chain reaction.

q: Why is carbon monoxide the deadliest product of combustion for people in a burning building?
a: It binds with hemoglobin more readily than oxygen does
It is the hottest gas produced by the fire
It produces a strong smell that causes panic
It is heavier than the smoke and stays on the floor
r: CO combines with hemoglobin far more readily than oxygen, starving the body of oxygen.
Its danger is chemical, not its temperature.
CO is colorless and odorless.
CO's density is close to air; its danger is its effect on blood.
e: Many fire deaths are caused by smoke inhalation rather than burns.

q: A burning house sets fire to another house across the street, though nothing touched it. How was the heat transferred?
a: Radiation
Conduction
Convection
Direct flame contact
r: Radiation transfers heat through electromagnetic waves across space without contact.
Conduction needs direct contact through a material.
Convection moves heat through moving gases or liquids, mainly upward.
The houses did not touch, so there was no flame contact.
e: Firefighters protect exposures by cooling them with water.

q: In a burning room, all the combustible contents suddenly ignite at almost the same time. What stage has been reached?
a: Flashover
Incipient stage
Decay stage
Smoldering ignition
r: Flashover is the sudden, near-simultaneous ignition of a room's contents, marking the change to a fully developed fire.
The incipient stage is the early stage of a small fire.
The decay stage is when the fire dies down.
Smoldering is slow combustion without flame.
e: Flashover is extremely dangerous to occupants and firefighters.

q: Why should water not be used on a fire involving live electrical equipment?
a: Water conducts electricity and can electrocute the firefighter
Water makes electrical fires spread to metals
Water reacts with plastic to form explosives
Water evaporates before it reaches the fire
r: Energized electrical fires (Class C) need non-conductive agents such as CO2 or dry chemical.
Water does not cause electrical fires to spread to metals.
Water does not form explosives with plastic.
Water reaches the fire; the danger is electric shock.
e: Once the power is cut, the fire may be fought according to the burning material.

q: A deep fryer of cooking oil catches fire in a restaurant kitchen. Which class of fire is it and what should be used?
a: Class K; a wet chemical extinguisher
Class A; a water extinguisher
Class C; a carbon dioxide extinguisher
Class D; a dry powder agent
r: Fires in cooking oils and fats are Class K, best fought with wet chemical agents that cool and seal the oil.
Water on burning oil causes violent splattering.
Class C is for energized electrical fires.
Class D is for combustible metals.
e: Many commercial kitchens have built-in wet chemical suppression systems.

q: Magnesium shavings catch fire in a machine shop. Which class of fire is it and what agent should be used?
a: Class D; a dry powder agent
Class B; foam
Class A; water
Class K; a wet chemical
r: Burning combustible metals are Class D fires, fought with special dry powders.
Foam is for flammable liquids.
Water can react violently with burning metals.
Wet chemical agents are for cooking oils.
e: Class D agents smother the fire and absorb heat.

q: A building uses fire-rated walls and self-closing fire doors to keep a fire in one area. What kind of fire protection is this?
a: Passive fire protection
Active fire protection
Manual fire suppression
Automatic fire detection
r: Passive protection uses building features that contain fire and smoke without needing activation.
Active protection needs action, such as sprinklers or alarms.
Manual suppression is firefighting by people.
Detection systems sense fire; they do not contain it.
e: Compartmentation slows fire spread and protects escape routes.
l: R.A. 9514 (Fire Code of the Philippines) and its IRR

q: Smoke from cooking keeps setting off the smoke detector in a canteen kitchen. Which detector is more suitable there?
a: Heat detector
Ionization smoke detector
Photoelectric smoke detector
Beam smoke detector
r: Heat detectors respond to temperature, so cooking smoke does not set them off.
Ionization detectors respond strongly to fine smoke particles.
Photoelectric detectors still respond to smoke.
Beam detectors also sense smoke.
e: The detector should fit the normal conditions of the area.

q: A man set fire to his own house, which stood close to his neighbors' houses, exposing them to danger. Is he liable for arson?
a: Yes, burning one's own property is arson if it endangers others
No, because a person may do as he wishes with his own property
No, unless one of the neighbors' houses actually burned
Yes, but only for malicious mischief
r: P.D. 1613 punishes burning one's own property under circumstances that expose another to danger.
Ownership does not allow endangering others.
The crime is complete when the danger is created.
The act is arson under the special law, not malicious mischief.
e: If he burned it to collect insurance, that is a special aggravating circumstance.

q: A store fire started at several points at the same time, and cans of gasoline were found inside. What do these facts establish under P.D. 1613?
a: Prima facie evidence of arson
Conclusive proof that the owner is guilty
Proof that the fire was accidental
Nothing, unless the owner confesses
r: Section 6 of P.D. 1613 lists multiple points of origin and the presence of flammable substances not normally found there as prima facie evidence of arson.
Prima facie evidence may be rebutted; it is not conclusive.
These facts point away from an accident.
Prima facie evidence stands without a confession.
e: The investigator must still identify the person responsible.

q: A man set fire to a house to kill the person inside, and the person died. What crime was committed?
a: Murder, because fire was the means to kill
Arson only, because the house was burned
Arson with homicide, a special complex crime
Homicide, because fire is not a qualifying circumstance
r: When the main objective is to kill and fire is the means, the crime is murder qualified by the use of fire.
When the main objective is to burn and death results, the crime is arson; here the aim was to kill.
Jurisprudence does not treat this as a special complex crime of arson with homicide.
Fire is a qualifying circumstance of murder under Article 248.
e: The offender's main objective decides between arson and murder (People v. Malngan).
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 248; People v. Malngan, G.R. No. 170470 (2006)

q: A V-shaped burn pattern appears on a wall at a fire scene. What does its lowest point usually indicate?
a: The area where the fire probably started
The point where the fire was finally put out
The place where the fire was coolest
The spot where firefighters entered
r: Fire rises and spreads outward, so the bottom of the V often points toward the origin.
Extinguishment does not create V patterns.
The base of the V is often where the fire burned longest.
Entry points do not make V patterns.
e: Patterns must be read together with other evidence, since ventilation can alter them.

q: An investigator sees an irregular burn on a floor shaped like spilled liquid. What should he do?
a: Collect debris in an airtight metal can for laboratory analysis
Conclude at once that gasoline was used
Wash the floor to see the pattern better
Ignore it, because floors always burn this way
r: Such patterns may suggest a flammable liquid, but only laboratory analysis of sealed samples can confirm it.
A pattern alone is not proof of an accelerant.
Washing destroys the evidence.
The pattern is worth investigating, not ignoring.
e: Airtight containers keep volatile residues from evaporating.

q: Why is the area of deepest and lowest charring often taken as a sign of the fire's origin?
a: The fire usually burned longest where it started
Fire always starts at the ceiling and burns downward
Charring is deepest where water was sprayed
The deepest char always marks where the accelerant was poured
r: The origin has often been exposed to fire the longest, so damage there tends to be deepest and lowest.
Fire usually spreads upward and outward.
Water reduces charring rather than deepening it.
Deep char does not by itself prove an accelerant.
e: Ventilation and fuel load can create misleading patterns, so investigators test their hypotheses.

q: Why is alcoholism regarded as a disease and not merely a bad habit?
a: It involves loss of control, physical dependence and withdrawal
It affects only persons who drink once a year
It can be cured simply by willpower in one day
It has no effect on the drinker's health or family
r: Alcoholism is marked by compulsive drinking, loss of control, tolerance and withdrawal symptoms.
Occasional drinking is not alcoholism.
Recovery usually requires treatment and support over time.
Alcoholism harms health, work and family life.
e: Treatment and rehabilitation are part of the response to alcoholism.

q: A man collects bets for a jueteng operator in his barangay. Which law punishes him?
a: R.A. 9287, which raised penalties for illegal numbers games
R.A. 9165, the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act
R.A. 10586, the Anti-Drunk Driving Act
R.A. 11313, the Safe Spaces Act
r: R.A. 9287 amended P.D. 1602 and punishes collectors, agents and others in illegal numbers games such as jueteng.
R.A. 9165 concerns dangerous drugs.
R.A. 10586 concerns driving under the influence.
R.A. 11313 concerns gender-based sexual harassment.
e: Penalties are higher for financiers, maintainers and protectors, including public officials.

q: Police rescue women whom a pimp forced into prostitution while keeping their earnings. How should the women be treated?
a: As victims of trafficking entitled to protection and services
As offenders to be charged for prostitution
As witnesses only, then released without assistance
As accomplices of the pimp
r: The anti-trafficking law treats trafficked persons as victims, not offenders, and provides them with protection and services.
Trafficked persons are not penalized for acts done as a result of being trafficked.
Victims are entitled to support, not just release.
Victims are not accomplices of their trafficker.
e: The pimp may be prosecuted for trafficking in persons.
l: R.A. 9208, as amended by R.A. 10364 and R.A. 11862

q: Why is shabu (methamphetamine hydrochloride) classified as a stimulant?
a: It speeds up the central nervous system
It slows down breathing and causes deep sleep
It causes users to see things that are not there only
It has no effect on the nervous system
r: Methamphetamine excites the central nervous system, causing wakefulness, energy and loss of appetite.
Slowing breathing and causing sleep describe depressants such as opioids.
Hallucinations can occur, but the main effect is stimulation.
Shabu strongly affects the nervous system.
e: Shabu is the most commonly abused dangerous drug in the Philippines.

q: A suspect has not slept for days, talks very fast, has dilated pupils and has lost much weight. Which drug use do these signs suggest?
a: Methamphetamine (shabu)
Heroin (opioid)
Marijuana (cannabis)
Morphine (opiate)
r: Sleeplessness, rapid speech, dilated pupils and weight loss are signs of stimulant use such as shabu.
Heroin causes drowsiness and pinpoint pupils.
Marijuana causes red eyes, increased appetite and relaxation.
Morphine causes drowsiness and constricted pupils.
e: Signs and symptoms help officers decide whether a drug test is warranted.

q: A person has pinpoint pupils, is very drowsy, and has needle marks on his arms. Which drug use do these signs suggest?
a: Heroin
Cocaine
Shabu
Ecstasy
r: Opioids such as heroin cause constricted pupils and drowsiness; injection leaves needle marks.
Cocaine is a stimulant that dilates the pupils.
Shabu is a stimulant that dilates the pupils.
Ecstasy is a stimulant that dilates the pupils.
e: Opioid overdose can stop breathing and is treated with naloxone.

q: A student has red eyes, a big appetite, a distorted sense of time, and a smell of burnt leaves on his clothes. Which drug use do these signs suggest?
a: Marijuana
Heroin
Cocaine
Inhalants
r: Red eyes, increased appetite, altered time perception and the smell of burnt plant matter are signs of marijuana use.
Heroin causes drowsiness and pinpoint pupils.
Cocaine causes excitement and dilated pupils.
Inhalants leave a chemical smell, such as solvent or glue.
e: Marijuana and marijuana resin are dangerous drugs under R.A. 9165.

q: A teenager inhales the vapors of a contact cement from a plastic bag. How is this drug use classified?
a: Inhalant (volatile solvent) abuse
Narcotic injection into a vein
Stimulant ingestion
Hallucinogen smoking
r: Sniffing glue or solvents from a bag is inhalant abuse.
No injection is involved.
The method is inhalation, and solvents are mainly depressants.
Smoking is not the method used here.
e: Inhalants can cause sudden death and brain damage.

q: What does the chain of custody of seized drugs cover?
a: Every recorded movement of the drugs from seizure to court and destruction
Only the transfer from the arresting officer to the prosecutor
Only the time the drugs spend inside the laboratory
Only the moment of arrest of the accused
r: Chain of custody covers the duly recorded custody of the drugs from seizure, to the laboratory, to safekeeping, to court presentation and destruction.
The chain covers more than one transfer.
The laboratory is only one link.
The arrest is only the start.
e: Each person who handled the item should be able to account for it.
l: Dangerous Drugs Board Regulation No. 1, s. 2002

q: Who should mark the seized sachets of drugs in a buy-bust operation, and when?
a: The seizing officer, immediately upon seizure, before the accused
The laboratory chemist, a week after receiving them
The prosecutor, when the case is filed in court
Any bystander, at the police station
r: Marking by the apprehending officer right after seizure, in the presence of the accused, starts the chain of custody.
Marking must happen at the time of seizure, not later at the laboratory.
The prosecutor does not mark evidence.
Only the officers handling the evidence mark it.
e: Marking separates the seized items from other similar items.
l: R.A. 9165, Sec. 21, as amended by R.A. 10640

q: During the inventory of seized drugs, which persons must witness it under R.A. 9165 as amended?
a: The accused or counsel, an elected official, and the NPS or media
Only the arresting officers and the team leader
Only the barangay tanods of the area
The accused's relatives and his employer
r: As amended by R.A. 10640, the inventory is done with the accused or his representative or counsel, an elected public official, and a representative of the National Prosecution Service or the media.
Officers alone do not satisfy the witness requirement.
Tanods are not among the required witnesses.
Relatives and employers are not required witnesses.
e: The witnesses must sign the inventory and be given a copy.
l: R.A. 9165, Sec. 21(1), as amended by R.A. 10640

q: Within what period after seizure must the drugs be submitted to the PDEA forensic laboratory?
a: 24 hours
48 hours
72 hours
7 days
r: Section 21(2) requires submission within 24 hours from seizure for qualitative and quantitative examination.
48 hours is longer than the law allows.
72 hours is longer than the law allows.
Seven days is far longer than the law allows.
e: Prompt submission protects the integrity of the evidence.

q: No elected official witnessed the inventory because none could be found despite real efforts. What is the effect on the seizure?
a: It is not void if the reason is proven and integrity is kept
It is always void, whatever the reason
It is valid even without any reason
It makes the drugs inadmissible but the arrest valid
r: The saving clause excuses non-compliance on justifiable grounds, as long as the integrity and evidentiary value of the items were preserved.
The law allows justified departures from the procedure.
The prosecution must prove the justifiable ground and the earnest efforts made.
Admissibility follows from whether the saving clause is satisfied.
e: The Supreme Court requires proof of earnest efforts to secure the witnesses (People v. Lim).
l: R.A. 9165, Sec. 21(1), as amended by R.A. 10640; People v. Lim, G.R. No. 231989 (2018)

q: In a buy-bust, the suspect handed a sachet of shabu to the poseur-buyer in exchange for marked money. What offense was committed?
a: Illegal sale of dangerous drugs (Section 5)
Illegal possession of dangerous drugs (Section 11)
Use of dangerous drugs (Section 15)
Maintenance of a drug den (Section 6)
r: Delivering the drug for payment completes the illegal sale.
Possession is a separate offense; the sale is proven by the transaction.
Use requires a positive drug test.
A drug den is a place where drugs are used or sold.
e: The elements of sale are the identity of buyer and seller, the object, the consideration, and the delivery and payment.

q: During a lawful search incident to arrest, police find sachets of shabu in the suspect's pocket. No sale took place. What offense applies?
a: Illegal possession of dangerous drugs (Section 11)
Illegal sale of dangerous drugs (Section 5)
Importation of dangerous drugs (Section 4)
Possession of drug paraphernalia (Section 12)
r: Possession without authority of a dangerous drug, knowingly and freely, is illegal possession.
There was no sale.
There was no bringing of drugs into the country.
Paraphernalia are instruments for using drugs, not the drugs themselves.
e: The penalty depends on the quantity of the drug.

q: What is the jurat of an affidavit?
a: The certificate that the affiant personally swore to it before the officer
The first paragraph stating the affiant's name and address
The list of evidence attached to the affidavit
The signature of the investigator who typed it
r: The jurat certifies that the affidavit was subscribed and sworn to before the administering officer.
The opening paragraph is the preliminary or introductory statement.
Attachments are annexes, not the jurat.
The typist's signature is not the jurat.
e: An affidavit is a written statement of facts made under oath.

q: Why must police blotter entries be made promptly and never erased?
a: The blotter is an official record whose integrity must be protected
Erasures make the blotter easier to read
Entries can be changed freely before the case reaches court
The blotter is a private notebook of the desk officer
r: The blotter is the official daily record of incidents, and late entries or erasures cast doubt on it.
Erasures reduce, not increase, reliability.
Changes must be made by proper correction, not freely.
The blotter is an official record, not a private notebook.
e: Corrections are made by a single line through the error, with the officer's initials.

q: An investigator is drafting a witness's sworn statement. In which part should the facts the witness personally saw be written?
a: Body
Jurat
Title
Signature block
r: The body states the facts known to the affiant, often in question-and-answer form.
The jurat is the officer's certification of the oath.
The title identifies the document.
The signature block holds the affiant's signature.
e: The body should state facts, not opinions or hearsay.

q: A party wants the court to postpone a scheduled hearing. Which pleading or paper should be filed?
a: Motion
Manifestation
Petition
Affidavit
r: A motion is an application for relief, such as postponement, other than by a pleading.
A manifestation informs the court of a fact without asking for relief.
A petition starts a special civil action or proceeding.
An affidavit is a sworn statement of facts.
e: A motion should state the relief sought and the grounds.

q: A shooting occurred an hour ago, and the chief needs a first written account of it today. Which report should the investigator submit?
a: Spot report
Progress report
Final report
After-operations report
r: A spot report is the immediate first report of an incident, usually within 24 hours.
A progress report updates the case later.
A final report closes the investigation.
An after-operations report covers a planned police operation.
e: Spot reports give the chain of command early information.

q: Two weeks after a robbery, the investigator reports newly identified witnesses and a recovered vehicle. Which report is this?
a: Progress report
Spot report
Final report
Incident record form
r: A progress report gives developments in an ongoing case.
The spot report was the first report.
The final report is made when the case is closed or filed.
The incident record form is the initial record of the complaint.
e: Progress reports are submitted at intervals until the case is resolved.

q: Why should a spot report avoid conclusions about a suspect's guilt?
a: The early facts may be incomplete, and guilt is for the court
Spot reports are always kept secret from the chief
Conclusions are allowed only in traffic accident reports
The suspect must first approve the report
r: A spot report records known facts early; unverified conclusions can mislead and prejudice the case.
Spot reports go to the chain of command.
Conclusions about guilt are not proper in any police report.
Suspects do not approve police reports.
e: Reports should be accurate, brief, complete and objective.

q: A case has been filed in court. Which report summarizes the whole investigation, the evidence and the disposition?
a: Final investigation report
Spot (initial) report
Progress report
Blotter entry
r: The final investigation report pulls together the facts, evidence, findings and action taken.
The spot report is the early first report.
Progress reports cover interim developments.
A blotter entry is a brief record of an incident.
e: The case folder holds the final report with the affidavits and other documents.

q: A regional director wants to issue a policy that all units must follow until it is revoked. Which issuance is most appropriate?
a: Memorandum circular
Special order (SO)
Travel order
Spot report
r: A memorandum circular states policies or rules of general and continuing application.
A special order covers specific personnel actions such as assignments and details.
A travel order authorizes official travel.
A spot report is an incident report, not an issuance.
e: Choosing the right issuance makes its scope and authority clear.

q: Which is the best opening paragraph for a memorandum order directing all station commanders to intensify checkpoints during the holidays?
a: 'All station commanders shall intensify checkpoints from Dec. 15 to Jan. 5 to prevent crime.'
'It has come to our attention that checkpoints are sometimes held and may be useful.'
'Checkpoints are important, and everyone should think about doing more of them.'
'The director feels that the holidays are very busy and requests suggestions.'
r: A good directive states who must act, what to do, when and why, in clear terms.
This wording is vague and gives no directive.
This wording gives no clear instruction or period.
This asks for suggestions instead of giving the order.
e: Administrative issuances should be clear, specific and enforceable.

q: Under R.A. 10175, what is illegal access?
a: Accessing all or part of a computer system without right
Selling a computer with an expired warranty
Posting a true story about oneself online
Using public Wi-Fi in a mall
r: Illegal access is accessing all or part of a computer system without right.
Selling equipment is not a cybercrime.
Posting true facts about oneself is not illegal access.
Using a public network with permission is not illegal access.
e: Other offenses against confidentiality include illegal interception and data interference.

q: Under R.A. 9003, which act involving solid waste is prohibited?
a: Open burning of solid waste
Segregating waste at the source
Composting biodegradable waste
Bringing recyclables to a materials recovery facility
r: R.A. 9003 prohibits the open burning of solid waste.
Segregation at the source is required, not prohibited.
Composting is encouraged.
Materials recovery facilities are part of the law's system.
e: R.A. 9003 is the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000.

q: Why does the Fisheries Code punish fishing with explosives?
a: It destroys coral reefs and kills marine life without discrimination
It is noisy and disturbs nearby coastal residents
It uses more fuel than ordinary fishing methods
It catches too few fish to be worth the cost
r: Blast fishing destroys habitats and kills fish of all sizes, harming fisheries for years.
The harm punished is ecological, not noise.
Fuel use is not the reason for the prohibition.
Blast fishing kills many fish; the problem is the destruction.
e: The Fisheries Code (R.A. 8550, as amended by R.A. 10654) also punishes fishing with noxious substances.

q: Police lawfully seized a suspect's phone during his arrest. Under the Rule on Cybercrime Warrants, what is needed to examine its data?
a: A Warrant to Examine Computer Data (WECD)
A Warrant to Intercept Computer Data (WICD)
A Warrant to Disclose Computer Data (WDCD)
No warrant, since the phone was lawfully seized
r: When a device was lawfully obtained by other means, a WECD is needed before its data are examined.
Interception concerns data in transmission.
Disclosure orders a person or provider to hand over data.
Lawful seizure of the device does not authorize examining its data.
e: The Rule on Cybercrime Warrants is A.M. No. 17-11-03-SC.
l: Rule on Cybercrime Warrants, A.M. No. 17-11-03-SC, Rule 6

q: Why should a running computer at a crime scene not simply be switched off?
a: Volatile data in memory would be lost
The computer would lock the police out forever
Switching it off deletes the hard disk at once
The computer would send an alarm to the suspect
r: Data held in memory, such as running processes and open sessions, disappear when power is cut; trained responders decide how to capture them.
Switching off does not always cause a lockout, though encryption may be a concern.
Turning off does not erase the disk.
Switching off does not send alarms.
e: Basic incident response includes documenting the screen and calling digital forensic specialists.

q: Why do examiners compute a hash value of a forensic image of a hard disk?
a: To prove the copy is identical to the original
To make the image file smaller for storage
To hide the image from the defense lawyers
To recover deleted files automatically
r: A matching hash shows the image is an exact, unchanged copy, which supports authentication in court.
Hashing does not compress files.
Evidence is disclosed according to the rules, not hidden.
Hashing does not recover files.
e: Examinations are done on the image, not on the original device.
l: Rules on Electronic Evidence, A.M. No. 01-7-01-SC

q: Police need a service provider to disclose the subscriber details and traffic data of an account used in online scams. Which warrant should they apply for?
a: Warrant to Disclose Computer Data (WDCD)
Warrant to Intercept Computer Data (WICD)
Warrant to Examine Computer Data (WECD)
Ordinary search warrant under Rule 126
r: A WDCD orders a person or provider to disclose subscriber information, traffic data or relevant data in its control.
Interception is for data in transmission.
A WECD is for examining data in a lawfully seized device.
Computer data are covered by the special warrants of the Rule.
e: R.A. 10175 also allows orders to preserve data while a warrant is sought.
l: Rule on Cybercrime Warrants, A.M. No. 17-11-03-SC, Rule 4

q: Under the Rules of Procedure for Environmental Cases, who may file a criminal complaint for violation of an environmental law?
a: An offended party, a peace officer, or an officer enforcing that law
Only the Secretary of Environment and Natural Resources
Only persons who own land near the polluted area
Only lawyers accredited by the Supreme Court
r: The Rules allow any offended party, peace officer, or public officer charged with enforcing an environmental law to file a criminal complaint.
The DENR Secretary is not the only one allowed.
Ownership of nearby land is not required.
No accreditation of lawyers is required.
e: The Rules are A.M. No. 09-6-8-SC.
l: Rules of Procedure for Environmental Cases, A.M. No. 09-6-8-SC, Rule 9

q: What is a citizen suit under the Rules of Procedure for Environmental Cases?
a: A suit by any Filipino, even for future generations
A suit that only government agencies may file
A suit filed only to collect taxes from polluters
A suit that may be filed only by foreign residents
r: Any Filipino citizen, in representation of others including minors and generations yet unborn, may file an action to enforce environmental laws.
Citizen suits are filed by citizens, not only by agencies.
Citizen suits enforce environmental rights, not taxes.
Citizen suits are for Filipino citizens.
e: This reflects the principle of intergenerational responsibility (Oposa v. Factoran).
l: Rules of Procedure for Environmental Cases, A.M. No. 09-6-8-SC, Rule 2, Sec. 5

q: In environmental cases, what is a SLAPP?
a: A lawsuit meant to harass those who protect the environment
A permit to build a landfill near a river
A warrant to search a factory suspected of polluting
A fine imposed on smoke-belching vehicles
r: A Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation is meant to harass or silence those enforcing environmental laws; the Rules allow it to be raised as a defense.
SLAPP is not a permit.
SLAPP is not a warrant.
SLAPP is not a fine.
e: A SLAPP defense may lead to dismissal and damages.
l: Rules of Procedure for Environmental Cases, A.M. No. 09-6-8-SC, Rule 6
